title: The Correction Which Was Not an Apology
memory_text: I wrote to Jolivet demanding that he distinguish the proposed reproduction of organized life from any claim that I had accomplished it. He replied with courtesy and pointed to the very paragraph in which he had already made that distinction. There was nothing to correct. I held the letter near the lamp, where the watermark showed through, searching for an insolent expression. I found none. I wrote a second letter about his insinuations concerning responsibility, one whose severity would have done honor to an unhappy prosecutor. It remained on my desk unsent. What I wanted, as I knew even then, was not merely a correction in the newspaper. I wanted another of those unhurried conversations in which he had seemed to find me amusing and important. The letter requested no such thing. At last I put his answer among my offprints. I told myself I had preserved the evidence of his journalistic cunning. I had also preserved his handwriting.

observations: Reporter had explicitly disclaimed any actual creation of life
decisions: Retain reply, withhold hostile second letter
consequences: Emotional wound persisted despite absence of factual grounds for retraction
belief_changes: Journalism can convey a fair account without producing a comfortable portrait
relationship_changes: Unreciprocated interest became confused with disappointment
alternative_interpretation: Jolivet's reply may have been no more than ordinary professionalism
interpretation_at_event: I thought I had been cruelly represented
later_reappraisal: I had wanted an apology for feelings the reporter had not caused

title: The Invitation Withdrawn
memory_text: The proposed lecture had been arranged by a gentleman who wrote of natural philosophy in one paragraph and of his parish in the next. His second letter arrived with a courtly regret: members of the society had become uncertain whether my paper affirmed the immortality of the soul. I had affirmed nothing of the kind and had spent a considerable sum explaining that exact point. I announced at supper that I did not require the approval of any gathering afraid of its own questions. Clara asked whether I had been looking forward to the lecture. I said, 'Naturally not,' with such force that she passed me the salt instead of answering. In my pocket was the timetable for the journey I should no longer make. I kept it until the paper wore through at its fold. The lost invitation was not the beginning of a universal prohibition. Two other men still wrote to me about the measurements. The absence of a particular room troubled me because I had already pictured myself standing at its centre.

observations: Patron withdrew invitation after seeing the public controversy
decisions: Refuse to petition for renewed invitation
consequences: First small reputational cost, not a decisive academic sanction
belief_changes: Loss of an audience can sting even when one despises its judgement
alternative_interpretation: The society may genuinely have misread the original paper independent of the interview
interpretation_at_event: I claimed not to care about small-minded patrons
later_reappraisal: I had rehearsed that lecture long before its cancellation

title: The Rumour Finds a Vocabulary
memory_text: A crate from Lenz's workshop gave out a knocking sound when a porter lifted it. The noise came from a loose cleat, but by the time the tale reached the faculty it involved a small beating heart. Kappel proposed allowing someone unconnected with the experiments to examine the room. I refused. The private work was not ready, and no journalist had earned the right to inspect it merely by putting me in print. Kappel asked why I was arguing with him as though he were the reporter. I answered that the distinction between them had lately grown thin. This was unjust. I knew it while speaking. In the corridor a younger scholar remarked upon my opinion that nature might be constructed. He had not read the journal, only the newspaper. I responded with a lecture on second-hand knowledge and watched him withdraw. The crate had done more immediate harm than the article. Yet the article had taught those hearing the crate what sort of story to expect. I would later pretend the two matters formed a single conspiracy. They had scarcely needed to cooperate.

observations: A harmless sound became suspicious in light of his reported speculative ambition
decisions: Refuse neutral inspection and rebuke young scholar
consequences: Trust eroded through multiple ordinary incidents, not one single exposé
belief_changes: Public notoriety can prime interpretations of unrelated evidence
relationship_changes: Kappel's practical goodwill strained under accusations
alternative_interpretation: The faculty had asked about sealed deliveries before the interview
interpretation_at_event: I believed the newspaper had made my opponents
later_reappraisal: It had given old suspicions a new vocabulary

title: Good Company without a Defence
memory_text: Clara brought bread to the laboratory and discovered me composing another answer to a clerical critic. She read the first paragraph, set the bread beside my elbow, and said that I might finish my reply after eating. Lenz was repairing a fine joint in the neighbouring room; the flame made a brief blue column which threw our shadows against the door. We spoke not of newspapers but of a misbehaving specimen, the price of coal, and the Ballerina's extraordinary preference for one melody. I was laughing when I noticed that nobody at the table required me to justify the study of life. I had begun to think that every conversation must turn into a hearing. Clara asked whether Paris had been pleasant. I said that it had been, until certain persons discovered the profit to be made from clever questions. She did not pursue the matter. After they left I opened the article at its first paragraph and read only the praise. There are evenings on which one may choose a smaller injury. I had not yet learned the difference between forgiveness and postponement.

observations: Close colleagues continued affectionate, practical company

consequences: Recognition crisis did not wholly destroy pleasure, routine, or trust
belief_changes: A professional controversy need not define each relationship
relationship_changes: Clara and Lenz remained separate from the public conflict
alternative_interpretation: His apparent peace may have depended on selectively reading the article
interpretation_at_event: I could live above the criticism by not reading it
later_reappraisal: I was learning to ration the attention given to injuries

title: The Newspaper on the Committee's Table
memory_text: Heller came to examine matters which a philosopher should not have needed to explain under oath. The committee wanted records of apparatus, the supervision of assistants, and the safety of certain investigations whose nature had already inspired more rumour than fact. When I entered the waiting room the French clipping lay among the papers. I knew the page before I could read the type, for one corner had torn beside Jolivet's last paragraph. I asked whether an article by a journalist constituted a scientific accusation. Heller said that it did not, and moved it aside. The questions that followed concerned invoices, access to the workrooms, and decisions I had taken without adequate consultation. Several were fair. I answered all of them as though they were variations of the question about my soul. Afterward I recalled Heller's hand pushing the newspaper out of the centre of the table. At the time I took the gesture as proof that the proceedings were absurd. In truth, he had been showing me where the actual difficulty lay.

observations: Committee asked about real procedures, records and supervision, not merely press remarks

title: The Sentence with Other Causes
memory_text: The dismissal arrived in a thick official envelope. I knew the language before I had reached the signature: conduct, confidence, propriety, conditions of inquiry. Not one clause named Jolivet. I nevertheless thought of his quiet questions, and in my anger constructed a path from the café to this room as straight as a surveyor's line. Clara came to see that the living vessels travelled upright. Kappel brought a crate and said very little. I tried to make a joke about how the university had finally learned to produce a ghost, meaning a professor who remained after his chair had been removed. Nobody laughed. In the weeks that followed I named the article among the reasons I had been wronged. I did not name the locks, the refusals to admit witnesses, the injured assistants, or the documents in which I had preferred elegance to accountability. Those matters did not disappear because I could arrange my grievances in a more pleasing order. I took the blue ledger away and left the doors to others.

interpretation_at_event: Jolivet's article had begun my undoing
later_reappraisal: It was a spark in a room furnished with dry timber, some of it mine

title: The Article beside the Window
memory_text: The tower contained three rooms that remained reliably dry and many that did not. I placed the French newspaper beneath a stack of discarded proofs so the draft from the window would not carry it across the floor. Then I moved it to a drawer, then returned it to the table because I could not bear to have it mistaken for waste. Rain made a little channel under the outer door. The paper had acquired a stain at one corner and smelled of dust when opened. I attempted to write a corrected account of the interview, putting my finest arguments into answers I had not delivered. By midnight I had produced a conversation in which Jolivet was both humiliated and grateful. I knew it was an invention. I preserved the draft for an evening, then tore it into strips for the stove. The published account remained. I preferred my adversary dishonest; it was intolerably inconvenient that his questions had been good.

observations: Counterfactual replies could be composed but did not change what had been said
decisions: Destroy invented revised dialogue; preserve original newspaper
consequences: Object became recurring trigger for rumination and self-editing
belief_changes: An imagined victory is not a historical correction
relationship_changes: Jolivet became a recurrent imagined interlocutor, not an actual correspondent
alternative_interpretation: He may have destroyed the draft because he was bored, not self-critical
interpretation_at_event: I would write the interview properly at last
later_reappraisal: The invented answers told me more about my shame than about Jolivet

title: No Letter Sent to Paris
memory_text: A year after my removal I found an envelope addressed to Jolivet behind a book of anatomical plates. I had filled it with notes on a new test of excitability, thinking I might reopen correspondence on grounds that would be beyond personal misunderstanding. The address was accurate but the envelope had no stamp. I held it beside the stove while the glass warmed my other hand. The question was absurdly simple: did I wish to send him a scientific correction, or did I wish him to remember me? I did not settle it. I laid the notes in the blue ledger and put the envelope into the drawer where I kept receipts too important to discard and too unimportant to display. I had begun telling acquaintances that journalists were natural parasites upon genius. Yet I knew perfectly well that he had read every page I showed him. If a parasite could ask a better question than a professor, the definition required some attention. I let the envelope stay unstamped.

observations: Unsent letter concealed personal longing within scholarly purpose
decisions: Retain notes and leave envelope unposted
consequences: Attachment shifted into an enduring unrealized prospective action

alternative_interpretation: The letter may primarily express desire for scientific recognition
interpretation_at_event: I had no need to renew acquaintance
later_reappraisal: The missing stamp was a decision I made repeatedly

title: Mathilde's Shorter Sentence
memory_text: Mathilde Rosen was correcting a new pamphlet of mine when she asked why I had retained a clipping from Paris in the same packet as the proofs. I said it was evidence in a private professional dispute. She read the passage concerning the scientist's right to determine the purpose of his own inquiries, then held it against a sentence in my current essay. They were embarrassingly alike. 'You have been answering this man for five years,' she observed. I informed her that the resemblance was accidental. The type smelled of ink and the iron press made a steady noise below us. She removed one self-congratulatory adverb from the new sentence. I demanded it be restored, then let the correction stand after reading the line in proof. I had hired a printer and obtained a reader capable of detecting when my argument was an old quarrel disguised as new science. She never asked whether I had liked Jolivet. I should have resented such a question much less than I feared.

alternative_interpretation: Mathilde may have recognized style rather than hidden affection
later_reappraisal: She had caught a five-year habit in one unnecessary word

title: The Catalogue's Wrong Title
memory_text: A bookseller sent a catalogue in which my private work had been entered under a ridiculous heading among curiosities. I had an excellent mind to write an objection in twelve pages. While searching for the original publication date I found the 1867 offprint, still carrying the printer's fault in its heading, and the newspaper which had made me visible to readers who did not care about the difference between a spinal reflex and a marvel. I considered sending the bookseller Jolivet's feature as evidence that I had once enjoyed continental notice. What prevented me was the conclusion: the young professor was talented but governed poorly by his own will. Instead I enclosed the German paper alone. The bookseller amended the listing without apology. For the remainder of the afternoon I was disagreeably pleased that a name could be corrected by reference to a document rather than by performance of injured dignity. Then I performed it anyway to Clara over supper. She asked whether the catalogue had been fixed. I admitted it had.

relationship_changes: Clara again separated practical resolution from grand rhetoric

interpretation_at_event: I refused a cheap form of self-promotion
later_reappraisal: I also feared what a new reader would conclude about me

title: The Widow's Unasked Question
memory_text: At a supper arranged by Matthias I spoke with a widow who had attended spiritualist meetings after her husband's death. She asked whether I believed anything of him had survived. I gave the answer I had given in print: the absence of a measurable substance did not demonstrate the absence of an immortal one. She thanked me for refusing an easy certainty, which was not the reaction I expected. A man nearby tried to enlist my authority for a plan to bring the dead into communication through electrical apparatus. I asked what observations would be taken if no voice appeared. He did not know. The widow said she did not intend to submit her husband's memory to an entertainer who could never admit failure. I remembered the critic in Paris asking who bore responsibility for what an experimenter made. For once I said little. The supper smelled of cabbage and candle wax. I went home with no new data and a genuine respect for a woman who had refused an offer she very much wanted to believe.

alternative_interpretation: His silence may be fatigue as well as newfound humility
interpretation_at_event: I had spared the woman a charlatan's confidence

title: The Margin Which Voss Would Not Close
memory_text: Voss found the French article while checking whether a passage from my old paper had been quoted honestly in a newer German essay. She read the portion concerning the obligations of a maker and asked why my reply had concerned the stupidity of regulations rather than the creature's possible sufferings. I began the familiar story of an ambitious journalist hunting scandal. She stopped me and asked which sentence Jolivet had invented. I could name none. I accused her of finding me too entertaining an enemy. She said that an interesting man and an adequate argument were separate objects. Then she returned to her botanical notes, leaving the newspaper open on the table. Later, while she measured a plant structure under poor light, I moved the lamp closer without speaking. Her thanks were casual. I remembered the reporter moving his chair to see my diagram and felt an old pang that was neither entirely anger nor desire. Perhaps being truly read is a form of intimacy to which I am unusually susceptible.

observations: Voss separated fairness of quoted text from moral adequacy of answer

title: Kappel's Inscribed Copy
memory_text: After Kappel's death I helped examine a box of his papers. Among careful notes and tedious requests from younger scholars lay my first offprint, the one I had inscribed for him in 1867. He had put it in a plain brown wrapper and marked the date in a small hand. There were corrections in the margins, none in his handwriting. I wondered whether he had lent the paper to someone who objected to my later conduct, or whether he himself had preserved the objections with the work. I should once have counted either possibility as disloyalty. Voss asked whether I wished to retain it. I said it belonged among Kappel's effects and placed it back with the other papers. I wanted him alive to dispute the decision. Outside, a cart wheel struck a stone and sounded for an instant like the metal apparatus I had used in youth. I stood with the wrapper in my fingers longer than the task required. This paper had been part of friendship before it had been part of a scandal.

interpretation_at_event: I wanted proof he had remained proud of me

title: Anna's Uncomfortable Standard
memory_text: Anna brought me an observation showing that a subject in a sealed chamber had repeatedly chosen the darker refuge after the light had been altered. I was pleased with the clarity of her records and tempted to order a more demanding series. She asked whether the increase in discomfort would justify a better result. The question was too close to Jolivet's for my taste, though she had never seen that article. I said that the scientist must not confuse the absence of speech with the absence of a claim. She seemed surprised to hear the words from me. I almost told her where I had first been pressed to explain them. Instead we revised the design to leave a clear way of withdrawing from the stimulus. Some useful observations were lost. Later I took the old newspaper from the drawer and found it less vicious than I remembered. It had never supplied this procedure; Anna had. The article's question endured without being the source of every good decision which followed.

interpretation_at_event: I called the design scientifically superior
later_reappraisal: Anna had made it more decent as well as more informative

title: The Rays Which Showed No Soul
memory_text: News of Röntgen's rays came through printed figures showing structures concealed by ordinary sight. A young man at a gathering asked whether such instruments would at last disclose the soul. I was amused to hear the old question dressed in the garments of a new discovery. We looked at a reproduced radiograph beneath a lamp. The paper showed the bones of a hand more clearly than the fingertips I placed upon its edge. I said the instrument was a triumph precisely because its evidence concerned something it had detected, not everything men desired it to detect. An acquaintance who remembered my old paper asked whether I had abandoned the search. I told him I had abandoned very little; I had merely become more particular about what a picture proves. At home I examined the French clipping, then the original German text. One contained a question about the possession of life; the other a question about its measurable conditions. They were related, not interchangeable. It had taken me longer than I liked to admit to make the distinction without contempt.

title: The Page I No Longer Folded Away
memory_text: The newspaper had grown brittle where it had been folded in Paris. It no longer opened without a warning at the crease. I spread it on the desk and weighted the corners with two glass stops, as I once weighted the pages of a laboratory record. There was no need to read it. I knew the questions, my evasions, the gracious opening, and the sentence about a will that could not govern itself. For many years I had blamed the article for showing the university the sort of man it ought to fear. Then I blamed myself for giving an intelligent reporter the very answers he was bound to print. Both accounts were too simple. The faculty had its reasons, some petty, some legitimate; I had made my own injuries, and others had been inflicted upon me. Jolivet had listened carefully. I still remembered his hand beside the diagram and the pleasure of Paris before any criticism. I replaced the folded sheet in the blue ledger. I did not forgive him, for I no longer knew which of his actions required forgiveness. I did not discard him either.
